title: An Equilibrium Constant is a Function of Temperature Only
lead: At equilibrium the reaction quotient takes a fixed value, the equilibrium constant. Its link to the standard reaction Gibbs energy tells how it moves with temperature, why compressing a gas mixture shifts the equilibrium without changing it, and how it reads in concentrations.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page.

exercises.source_id: Consider the reaction of ammonia decomposition
exercises.prompt:
Consider the reaction of ammonia decomposition:

$$ \sf 2NH_3\it\left(g\right)\sf\leftrightharpoons N_2\it\left(g\right)\sf+3H_2\it\left(g\right) $$ $$ \Delta_fH^{\circ}(\text{NH}_3, g)=-45.90\;\sf kJ/mol $$

The reaction is initially at equilibrium. For each of the stresses, use your General Chemistry knowledge to decide if equilibrium will be unaffected, or if it will shift towards reactants or products.

ProcessShifts towards
Isothermal removal of $\sf H_2$ gas
Isothermal addition of $\sf N_2$ gas
Isothermal decrease of container volume
Isothermal and isochoric addition of argon gas
Isobaric increase of temperature

Write the equilibrium constant expression for the above chemical reaction in terms of gas-phase mole fractions.

answer.hint: Count the moles of gas on each side, and find the sign of the reaction enthalpy from the enthalpy of formation of NH₃.
answer.solution:
Removing H₂ lowers $Q$ below $K$, so the equilibrium shifts towards the products. Adding N₂ raises $Q$ above $K$, so it shifts towards the reactants. A smaller volume raises the total pressure, and the equilibrium moves to the side with fewer molecules: 2 mol of NH₃ against 4 mol of N₂ and H₂, so towards the reactants. Argon added at constant volume leaves every partial pressure as it was, so $Q$ still equals $K$ and the equilibrium is unaffected. The reaction enthalpy is $\kDeltarHstd = -2\times(-45.90) = +91.80$ kJ/mol, so the decomposition is endothermic, and by the van 't Hoff equation $K$ grows with temperature: the equilibrium shifts towards the products.

With $\kPpi = x_i\kP$,

$$ K = \dfrac{(P_{\text{N}_2}/P^\circ)(P_{\text{H}_2}/P^\circ)^3}{(P_{\text{NH}_3}/P^\circ)^2} = \dfrac{x_{\text{N}_2}\,x_{\text{H}_2}^3}{x_{\text{NH}_3}^2}\left(\dfrac{P}{P^\circ}\right)^2 $$
